<reflection>
- The second experiment successfully widened the NLL gap slightly, bringing models with substrate-dependent (M16, M7) and product-dependent (M17) interactions to the top, while penalizing simple models (M1) and catalyst-dimer models (M3, M4).
- However, the NLL differences are still relatively small (around 5 units). The models are still able to compensate for the changes in conditions.
- To definitively separate substrate-induced deactivation/inhibition (M16, M7) from product-induced deactivation (M17) and intrinsic intermediate deactivation (M14), we need an experiment that strongly amplifies substrate effects while delaying product effects.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
By using the maximum allowable substrate concentration (S = 5.0) and a low catalyst concentration (cat = 0.02) with no initial product (P = 0.0), we can strongly differentiate the leading mechanisms. 
For M16 (S + catS -> inactive), the high [S] and saturated [catS] will drive rapid deactivation, leading to an early plateau in product formation. 
For M11 (S + cat -> inactive), the high [S] will push the equilibrium towards catS, depleting free [cat] and potentially slowing down the deactivation compared to M16.
For M17 (P + catS -> inactive), the reaction will start at a normal rate and only slow down as product accumulates, showing a distinct curvature compared to the immediate deactivation of M16.
For M14 (catS -> inactive), the deactivation rate will be constant (since [catS] is saturated) and independent of the high [S], leading to a different plateau level.
The low catalyst concentration ensures the reaction occurs slowly enough to clearly observe the shape of the kinetic curve and any premature plateaus before the substrate is significantly depleted.
</hypothesis>
